summary:
Earth Information Jukebox transforms NASA’s Earth data into an interactive audio-visual experience. Using GOES-16 satellite imagery and NASA Earth Now weather and air-quality data, our website converts environmental changes into sound through pitch, rhythm, and tone, allowing users to hear how events like storms, heat waves, and pollution develop over time.

Inspired by a music player, users can select a dataset as a track, press play, and explore changes through a synchronized timeline where visuals and audio work together.

Accessibility is at the heart of our project. With keyboard controls, screen-reader labels, and an audio legend explaining each sound, we make Earth science more inclusive, particularly for blind and low-vision users.

Our mission is to make NASA’s Earth observations more accessible, engaging, and understandable by allowing people to not only see our changing planet but also hear it.
details:
Earth Information Jukebox – Project Description

Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web-based platform that transforms NASA's Earth observation data into an accessible audio-visual experience. Our project addresses the challenge of making scientific information understandable not only through visual representations but also through sound.

How Does It Work?

The platform uses GOES-16 ABI satellite imagery and NASA Earth Now weather and air-quality data. Users can select a dataset as a musical track, press play, and explore environmental changes over time. As the data changes, our system translates different values into musical elements such as pitch, rhythm, and tone. These sounds are synchronized with on-screen visuals, allowing users to hear and see how events such as storms, heat waves, and changes in air quality develop.

The jukebox-style interface allows users to select tracks, control playback, and navigate through timelines, making the experience familiar and easy to use.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our primary goal is to make Earth science more accessible, inclusive, and engaging. The project provides an alternative way of understanding complex environmental datasets, particularly benefiting blind and low-vision individuals who may face difficulties interpreting traditional charts, maps, and satellite images. It also helps other users recognize patterns and changes in environmental conditions through sound.

Tools and Technologies Used

We developed the platform using several technologies:

- React.js: Used to build the interactive frontend and user interface.
- Tone.js: Used for generating, controlling, and synchronizing audio.
- Express.js: Used for backend API and server functionality.
- Python: Used for processing NASA datasets.
- FFmpeg: Used to extract video frames for visualizations.

Our project integrates NASA's GOES-16 ABI satellite imagery and Earth Now weather and air-quality data. We also use the C Major Pentatonic scale to map environmental data values to musical notes, creating meaningful audio representations.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Earth Information Jukebox lies in its approach to data sonification. Instead of presenting scientific information through conventional charts and graphs alone, we turn real environmental datasets into musical experiences. Treating datasets as tracks in a jukebox makes scientific exploration more interactive, memorable, and engaging.

Factors Considered During Development

Throughout development, our team prioritized accessibility, simplicity, accurate representation of scientific data, synchronization between audio and visuals, and ease of navigation. We also considered users with different visual abilities and levels of scientific knowledge.

Ultimately, Earth Information Jukebox aims to bridge the gap between scientific data and human experience, allowing everyone to connect with our changing planet through both sight and sound.
